sections.content: This handbook outlines a homebrew tabletop roleplaying game system, combining the detailed mechanics of [GURPS 4th Edition](https://gurps.fandom.com/wiki/GURPS_Star_Wars) (unofficial SW Gamebook) with thematic elements and character archetypes of the [Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars:_Knights_of_the_Old_Republic_(video_game)) video game, set within the tumultuous [Mandalorian Wars era](https://starwars.fandom.com/wiki/Mandalorian_Wars) (approximately 3964 BBY). This period is defined by gritty, gray-morality, and war-driven themes, with growing Force-based mysticism and tragedy as the galaxy endures conflict and the lines between good and evil blur.
How to Play: The 3d6 Roll-Under Mechanic

The system utilizes the [GURPS 3d6 roll-under mechanic](https://www.google.com/search?q=gurps+3d6+roll-under+mechanic+explanation&client=firefox-b-1-d&sca_esv=9bb6a8d79ae60b0c&ei=uQQ3aPbGK66s5NoPyuLMgQ4&oq=GURPS+3d6+roll-under+mechanic+exp&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LXNlcnAiIUdVUlBTIDNkNiByb2xsLXVuZGVyIG1lY2hhbmljIGV4cCoCCAEyBRAhGKABMgUQIRigATIFECEYoAEyBRAhGKABMgUQIRigAUi7FVCVBljJC3ABeACQAQCYAVOgAfICqgEBNbgBA8gBAPgBAZgCBaACywLCAg4QABiABBiwAxiGAxiKBcICCxAAGIAEGLADGKIEwgIIEAAYsAMY7wXCAgUQIRirApgDAIgGAZAGBpIHATWgB98VsgcBNLgHxwLCBwUwLjQuMcgHCQ&sclient=gws-wiz-serp) as its foundation for all task resolution, providing a consistent probability curve and granular skill differentiation.

To perform an action with a chance of failure, roll three six-sided dice (3d6). If the total is less than or equal to your relevant Skill Level or Attribute Score, the action succeeds. The amount by which a roll succeeds or fails is its Margin: subtract the roll from the number you needed. A roll of 9 against a skill of 14 is a Margin of Success of 5; a roll of 16 against the same skill is a Margin of Failure of 2. Where a rule pays out per point of margin -- an extra salvaged part per 2 points, a defence penalty equal to your margin of victory -- this is the number it means.

content: Rolls of 3 or 4 are always critical successes. A 5 is a critical success if your effective skill is 15 or higher; a 6 is a critical success if it is 16 or higher.

Rolls of 17 or 18 always fail, whatever your effective skill. An 18 is always a critical failure. A 17 is a critical failure if your effective skill is 15 or lower; at 16 or higher it is an ordinary failure. Any roll that fails by 10 or more is also a critical failure.

sections.content: Attributes
The four primary attributes form the foundation of a character’s capabilities:

content: **Strength (ST):** Physical power, lifting capacity, melee damage.
**Dexterity (DX):** Agility, coordination, hand-eye precision, ranged attacks.
**Intelligence (IQ):** Mental acuity, knowledge, reasoning, most skills.
**Health (HT):** Stamina, resistance to injury, recovery, willpower (for some checks).

sections.content: Secondary Characteristics
Derived from attributes, these characteristics define a character’s baseline abilities and resources:

content: **Hit Points (HP):** Physical endurance and ability to withstand damage. When HP drops to 0 or below, a character is severely injured and risks unconsciousness or death.
**Will:** Mental fortitude, courage, focus, and the ability to resist intimidation, pain, and temptation. Derived from **IQ** by default.
**Perception (Per):** General awareness and ability to notice things using all your senses. Derived from **IQ** by default.

**Endurance Points (EP):** (Formerly “Fatigue Points”) This resource represents a character’s physical stamina and energy for strenuous actions, prolonged exertion, and certain combat maneuvers (e.g., All-Out Attacks, specific Martial Arts techniques).
When a character drops below 1/3rd their max EP, they must make a **HT** roll to perform strenuous actions, or fight effectively.

When EP drops to 0, the character suffers extreme fatigue, but is not immediately out of the fight. Any further strenuous activity requires a **Will** roll, on a failed roll at 0, the character loses consciousness.

When the character drops below 0 EP, for every point below zero, they lose 1 point from **ST**, **DX**, and **IQ** and must continue to make **Will** rolls. If any of these attributes drop to 0, the character instantly passes out.
Rest is the primary way to regain EP, and characters typically recover 1EP for every 10 minutes of quiet, restful activity. Alternatively, characters fully restore their EP upon a full night’s rest.

**Force Points (FP):** A dedicated resource for activating and sustaining Force powers. Force Points represent a Force-user’s connection to and mastery over the Force. Unlike Endurance Points, Force Points are specifically tied to a character’s Force Sensitivity and power. (Detailed further in **Chapter 8: Force Powers**).
FP returns at the rates in Chapter 8 (Gaining FP), or fully upon a full night’s rest.
**Basic Speed:** Derived from (**DX** + **HT**) / 4, this determines movement rate and combat initiative.
**Basic Move:** Derived from (**ST** + **DX**) / 4 (rounded down), this indicates ground movement speed in yards per second or yards per turn in combat.
**Damage Resistance (DR):** Protection provided by armor, natural toughness, or Force powers, reducing incoming damage.

sections.content: Hazards: Hunger, Thirst, and Disease

Two hazards come up often enough to need a standing rule rather than a fresh ruling each time. Both resolve with machinery already described above -- Endurance Points for going without, an HT roll for infection -- and both are what several pieces of gear in Chapter 10 exist to prevent.
Going Without Food or Water

A character who does not eat within a 24-hour period loses 1 EP, and 1 more for each further day without food. A character who does not drink loses 1 EP per 12 hours. EP lost this way cannot be recovered by rest until the character eats or drinks: the usual 1 EP per 10 minutes does not touch it, and a full night’s sleep restores them to that lowered ceiling rather than to full. Everything above about low and negative EP still applies, so a character who goes long enough without water will begin losing ST, DX and IQ and will eventually fall unconscious.
One pack of Field Rations (Chapter 10) covers a day’s food, as does a successful Survival roll for the terrain. Water must come from a safe source, or be made safe with a Water Purifier.
Eating Well

The other side of going without is eating well. A character who eats a proper prepared meal -- one cooked fresh with a Cooking roll, or a quality meal bought for the purpose -- becomes Well-Fed until their next meal, roughly a day. Only the best meal of a day counts, and being Well-Fed does not stack with itself or with the boosts of a battle stimulant.

How much good it does depends on the Cooking roll and the ingredients. A simple hot meal -- any successful Cooking roll, or a self-heating Hot Meal Pack (Chapter 10) -- leaves the eater Well-Fed and recovering Endurance Points from rest twice as fast, 1 EP every 5 minutes rather than 10. A good meal, cooked by 3 or more or made with fine ingredients, does that and adds +1 to Fright Checks and to any roll to resist fatigue until the next meal. A feast -- a Cooking critical success, a roll made by 3 or more with fine ingredients, or a Field Feast Kit (Chapter 10), and enough for the whole group -- does all of that, and each person who eats recovers 1 EP at once and takes +1 to their next Fright Check.

Ingredients set the ceiling. Rough fare, such as plain ration paste or foraged scraps, never rises above a simple meal however skilled the cook; ordinary ingredients reach a good meal; and only fine ingredients -- a named regional delicacy (Chapter 19), or a Field Feast Kit -- allow a feast.

A character with Survival can live off the land. One Survival roll for the terrain, once a day, feeds the forager and one more person for every 2 points the roll is made by, and yields fresh ingredients of ordinary quality -- rough in a barren waste, at the Gamemaster’s call. Water is found the same way, or made safe with a Water Purifier.

Fresh food, foraged or bought unpreserved, keeps about two days before it spoils -- less in jungle heat, longer in the cold. Cooking preserves it: the Rations & Preserved Food prepared with Cooking (Chapter 10) keep in the field indefinitely. Spoiled food feeds no one.
Disease & Infection

Disease is resolved the way poison is -- see the toxin entries in Chapter 10 -- as an HT roll at a penalty set by severity; any disease-resistance trait a character has adds its bonus to that roll. Exposure means contaminated food or water, a wound left untreated in the field, a parasite, or close quarters with someone already sick, and calls for one roll. Success: no effect. Failure: the character contracts it, and symptoms begin after the incubation below. Critical failure: as failure, one severity step worse.

Severity sets the penalty and the effect. Mild is HT-1 and leaves the character Nauseated (-2 to all attributes and skills). Serious is HT-3, Nauseated, and EP does not restore on rest. Severe is HT-5, Nauseated, no EP restoration, and 1 HP lost per day. Incubation is 1d hours for Mild and 1d days for Serious or Severe. A disease outside these three states its own penalty and effect the way a toxin does.

Shaking it off: a sick character rolls HT once per day at the same penalty. One success ends a Mild case; Serious and Severe need two consecutive successes. A critical failure worsens the case by one step. An Antidote Kit, or a successful Physician roll, grants +2 to these rolls.

A Water Purifier removes the roll entirely for anything waterborne -- that is what it is for. Every bonus that names disease adds to all of the rolls above: the Body Glove and Thermal Cloak’s +1 (Chapter 13), a species’ Resistant to Disease (Chapter 18), and the Immunity Implant’s +8 (Chapter 14). A droid, immune to metabolic hazards, never rolls at all.
Time

One ladder of time runs the game, from the split second of a blaster exchange to the years of galactic history. A combat turn is one second (Chapter 7); rest and short tasks run in minutes; the food, water, and air clocks in hours; and most of ordinary life -- meals, travel, healing, and work -- in days. A standard day is 24 standard hours, the galaxy’s chronometer day, and it is the unit the out-of-combat rules count in. Five days make a week, and the wider calendar is laid out for the Gamemaster in Chapter 20.
Day, Night, and Watches

A standard day splits into daylight and night. A world’s own cycle may be shorter or longer, but that is worldbuilding (Chapter 20); the rules count standard days. A party that must post a guard divides the night into as many watches as it has sentries, and a character who stands a watch gets that much less rest.
Rest and Recovery

A character recovers 1 EP for every 10 minutes of quiet rest, and FP at the rates in Chapter 8 (1 per hour of light activity, an eighth of maximum FP per hour of rest, 1 per 3 minutes of meditation). A full night’s sleep -- 8 hours of sleep or undisturbed rest -- restores both to full. Hit Points return more slowly: a wounded character who rests a full day rolls against HT at day’s end, recovering 1 HP on a success, or 3 with a Physician’s care or a medpac (Chapter 10), and simply holds steady on a failure.

A character who misses a full night -- standing watch, marching hard, or going hungry or thirsty -- restores EP and FP only in part, at the Gamemaster’s call, and heals no HP that day. A Caf Ration (Chapter 10) can take the edge off a short night.
